title: Kernel Density Estimation & Local Smoothing
excerpt: Kernel density estimation draws a smooth curve to summarize where observations are concentrated, without relying on fixed histogram bins. Compare smoothing settings to see how too much or too little smoothing can hide peaks, exaggerate noise and change the apparent tails.
objectives: Explain how kernel density estimation places and averages a small kernel around each observation.
Describe how kernel choice and bandwidth change the estimated density, including the bias–variance trade-off.
Interpret density values, modes, and interval probability without confusing height with probability.
Connect joint and conditional density estimates to Nadaraya–Watson and local polynomial regression.
Recognize boundary and high-dimensional limitations and use a rule of thumb as a starting point, not a verdict.

lessons.title: From a histogram to a smooth density
lessons.body:
A histogram groups observations into bins, so its appearance can change when the bin width or starting point changes. Kernel density estimation (KDE) instead centers a small, smooth function on every observation and adds the contributions. For observations x₁,…,xₙ and bandwidth h, a common one-dimensional estimate is f̂ₕ(y) = (1/(n h)) Σᵢ K((y − xᵢ)/h). Here K is the kernel shape and h controls its width. If K integrates to one, the estimate is a density: its total area is approximately one, while its height has units of 1/(the measurement unit).

Illustrative synthetic economic example (January–June 2025): suppose four fictional workers’ job-search durations, measured in weeks, are 2, 3, 3, and 5. To show the mechanics without hiding the calculation, use a uniform kernel K(u)=0.5 when |u|≤1 and 0 otherwise, with bandwidth h=1 week. At y=3 weeks, the observations at 2, 3, and 3 are within one bandwidth, while 5 is not, so f̂₁(3)=[0.5+0.5+0.5+0]/(4×1)=0.375 per week. The estimate is a smoothed description of concentration around three-week job searches: its height is density per week, not the probability of exactly three weeks. Probability for an interval would be represented by area under the curve over that interval.

A KDE can summarize where the selected job-search durations are concentrated and can make skewness or multiple local clusters easier to inspect than a single histogram, but it cannot establish the population distribution, explain why searches last longer, prove a policy caused a difference, or forecast an individual’s next duration. Treat bandwidth as a decision to check: compare a narrow, medium, and wide value, inspect whether apparent peaks persist, and consider boundary leakage because durations cannot be negative. A common mistake is reading a tall density value as a probability at one exact continuous duration; use area over a range instead. For implementation details and bandwidth context, see “Scikit-learn User Guide — Density Estimation” in the linked sources below.

KDE is especially useful when bin boundaries are arbitrary. Suppose five synthetic monthly commuting costs are 40, 42, 43, 60, and 61 currency units, and compare the local contribution at y=42 currency units using a uniform kernel with h=2 currency units. The standardized distances are (42−40)/2=1, (42−42)/2=0, (42−43)/2=−0.5, (42−60)/2=−9, and (42−61)/2=−9.5. With K(u)=0.5 for |u|≤1, the density is [0.5+0.5+0.5+0+0]/(5×2)=0.15 per currency unit. This height describes concentration near 42, not the chance of one exact cost. It also does not show why costs differ or support a causal claim. For implementation details, see “Scikit-learn User Guide — Density Estimation” in the linked sources.

To turn a KDE into a decision quantity, integrate it over the relevant return range rather than reading a curve height. Consider an explicitly illustrative synthetic sample of four daily changes, measured in percentage points: −1.0, 0.0, 0.5, and 1.5. With a Gaussian KDE and bandwidth h = 0.5 percentage points, the estimated probability of a non-positive change is the average of four standard-normal cumulative probabilities: [Φ((0−(−1.0))/0.5) + Φ((0−0.0)/0.5) + Φ((0−0.5)/0.5) + Φ((0−1.5)/0.5)]/4 = [Φ(2)+Φ(0)+Φ(−1)+Φ(−3)]/4 ≈ (0.9772+0.5000+0.1587+0.0013)/4 = 0.4093, or about 40.9%. Thus the smoothed sample assigns roughly four in ten days to returns at or below zero, conditional on this bandwidth and sample—not a population frequency or forecast. The Gaussian kernel also assigns some mass beyond any finite boundary; for genuinely bounded outcomes, inspect boundary bias or use a suitable transformation. Changing h changes this area, so report it alongside the smoothing choice.
lessons.formula: f̂ₕ(y) = (1 / (n h)) Σᵢ K((y − xᵢ) / h)
lessons.takeaway: A KDE is a sum of little contributions centered on the observed data; it does not create new observations.

practice.question: If returns are measured in percentage points, what does the vertical axis of a one-dimensional density plot represent?
practice.hint: A density is normalized by area, so its units are the inverse of the horizontal-axis units.
practice.solution: It is density per percentage point, not a probability at one exact return. Probability is represented by area over a range of returns.

lessons.title: What the kernel contributes
lessons.body:
A kernel is a weighting function. The supplied lecture describes a symmetric kernel with integral one, mean zero, and finite variance; common positive choices include Gaussian, triangular, and Epanechnikov shapes. In a standard positive-kernel KDE, nearby observations contribute more than distant ones. The kernel's exact shape usually matters less than the bandwidth, though shape and support affect smoothness and edge behavior. Higher-order kernels can use zero or negative weights to reduce some smoothing bias, but the resulting estimate may dip below zero and is less intuitive; they are not the default beginner choice.

The kernel shape determines how quickly influence fades, even when the bandwidth is fixed. Consider three synthetic hourly wages, measured in currency units: 10, 12, and 16, and estimate at y=12 with h=4 currency units. The standardized distances are −0.5, 0, and 1. A triangular kernel K(u)=1−|u| for |u|≤1 gives weights 0.5, 1, and 0, so the unnormalized contributions are 0.5, 1, and 0; the observation at 16 is just at the support edge and contributes zero. A Gaussian kernel would give it a small positive contribution instead. Thus kernel choice changes local emphasis, while h sets the distance scale. This comparison is descriptive, assumes comparable wage measurements, and does not identify a wage-setting mechanism. For a reference implementation, see “SciPy Reference — gaussian_kde” in the linked sources.

To see the normalization and units, use an illustrative synthetic sample of four monthly inflation changes, measured in percentage points: −1, 0, 1, and 2, with Gaussian bandwidth h = 1 percentage point. At y = 0, the KDE is [φ(1) + φ(0) + φ(1) + φ(2)]/(4 × 1 pp), where φ(0) ≈ 0.39894, φ(1) ≈ 0.24197, and φ(2) ≈ 0.05399. The result is (0.24197 + 0.39894 + 0.24197 + 0.05399)/4 ≈ 0.23422 per percentage point. That is a density height, not a 23.422% chance of exactly zero inflation. For an interval, integrate the same four shifted normal kernels: the estimated probability of 0 ≤ Y ≤ 1 pp is [Φ(2)−Φ(1) + Φ(1)−Φ(0) + Φ(0)−Φ(−1) + Φ(−1)−Φ(−2)]/4 ≈ [0.13591 + 0.34134 + 0.34134 + 0.13591]/4 = 0.23863, or 23.863%. The calculation assumes comparable measurements and treats the sample as descriptive; changing h changes both local height and interval area allocation, while the full mixture still integrates to one over the whole real line.
lessons.formula: u = (y − xᵢ) / h  ·  nearby observations receive larger K(u)
lessons.takeaway: The kernel says how each point fades with distance; the bandwidth decides what counts as nearby.

practice.question: A symmetric kernel is centered on an observation. Which observation contributes more to the estimate at y: one very close to y or one far away?
practice.hint: Think about the kernel's weight as distance from its center grows.
practice.solution: The nearby observation usually contributes more. A Gaussian kernel never becomes exactly zero, while a compact-support kernel eventually gives distant points zero weight.

lessons.title: Bandwidth is the main smoothing decision
lessons.body:
A small h creates narrow bumps: genuine local structure may appear, but random wiggles can look like extra modes. A large h merges nearby features and can hide multiple peaks. This is the bias–variance trade-off: extra smoothness often raises smoothing bias while reducing sample-to-sample roughness. One familiar univariate normal-reference starting point is Silverman's rule h ≈ 1.06 s n⁻¹ᐟ⁵, where s is the sample standard deviation and n the number of observations. It is a rule of thumb, not a universal optimum; cross-validation and subject-matter checks can lead to a different choice. Compare several plausible bandwidths before telling a story about the number of modes.

Bandwidth sensitivity can be made concrete with the rule h≈1.06s n⁻¹ᐟ⁵. For a synthetic sample of n=32 quarterly inflation rates measured in percentage points, suppose the sample standard deviation is s=2 percentage points. Since 32^(−1/5) is approximately 0.5, the starting bandwidth is 1.06×2×0.5=1.06 percentage points. A bandwidth near 0.5 percentage points would show finer variation; one near 2 percentage points would merge features roughly two percentage points apart. These are smoothing distances, not inflation changes or probabilities. The calculation assumes the normal-reference rule is a reasonable starting approximation; it does not prove normality, select the true population bandwidth, or establish economic causes of peaks. Compare validation results and plots before interpreting modes. This is a univariate normal-reference rule, not a universal optimum. Defaults vary: SciPy’s gaussian_kde uses Scott’s factor by default, and its Silverman factor is a multivariate rule rather than this exact univariate formula. For the normal-reference derivation, see “Hyndman et al. — Normal Reference Rule for Kernel Density Estimation” and “Bruce Hansen — Kernel Density Estimation (normal-reference rule)”; for SciPy’s default, see “SciPy Reference — gaussian_kde.”

To turn a KDE into an interval summary, integrate the kernels rather than reading the curve’s height. Consider this explicitly synthetic example of eight daily return changes, in percentage points: −1.0, −0.6, −0.2, 0.1, 0.3, 0.8, 1.1, and 1.5, with Gaussian bandwidth h = 0.4 percentage points. For the interval [0, 1] percentage point, the estimated mass is (1/8) Σᵢ[Φ((1−xᵢ)/0.4) − Φ((0−xᵢ)/0.4)], where Φ is the standard-normal CDF. The eight kernel contributions are approximately 0.006, 0.067, 0.307, 0.586, 0.733, 0.669, 0.398, and 0.106; they sum to 2.873, so division by n gives 0.359, or 35.9% estimated mass. This is not the observed fraction in the interval (3/8 = 37.5%) and is not a probability that the next return will land there: smoothing reallocates weight across the boundaries. The calculation assumes these observations represent the target return distribution and that Gaussian smoothing is defensible. Recompute it for alternative h values; a materially different 35.9% figure signals bandwidth sensitivity, not a contradiction in the arithmetic.
lessons.formula: Normal-reference starting point: h ≈ 1.06 s n⁻¹ᐟ⁵
lessons.takeaway: Bandwidth is measured in the same units as the data and can change the story; always inspect sensitivity.

practice.question: Your KDE shows four small peaks with a very narrow bandwidth, but only one broad mound with a wider bandwidth. What should you conclude?
practice.hint: Ask whether the apparent structure is stable across reasonable smoothing choices.
practice.solution: Do not treat either curve as a verdict. The narrow curve may overfit sample noise and the wide one may oversmooth real subgroups. Show sensitivity, check the observations and use a defensible bandwidth rule or validation criterion.

lessons.title: Read the curve as a density, not a probability
lessons.body:
A density curve's height is not the probability of observing that exact continuous value. Probability over an interval is the area under the density across that interval. A high peak indicates that observations are concentrated nearby relative to other regions; it does not mean that the peak value is common as an exact outcome. KDEs can reveal skewness, multiple clusters, and tail shape that a single mean conceals. Near a hard boundary—such as a nonnegative duration—symmetric kernels can place some mass outside the allowed range, so consider boundary-aware methods or state the limitation.

To translate height into probability, use area and keep the horizontal units visible. Suppose a synthetic KDE for annual portfolio returns has an average estimated density of 0.08 per percentage point from −1% to 1%. The interval width is 1−(−1)=2 percentage points, so a simple rectangle approximation gives probability 0.08×2=0.16, or 16%. This is not the probability of an exact 0% return; a single point has zero width on a continuous scale. The 16% is only an approximation to the KDE area, conditional on the sample and smoothing choice. It does not guarantee that future returns follow the curve or establish that a portfolio policy caused returns. Boundary and tail behavior should be checked separately. For density-estimation details, see “SciPy Reference — gaussian_kde” in the linked sources.

For a concrete, synthetic calculation, take the lab’s first six displayed return changes, −2.80, −2.45, −2.20, −1.95, −1.72, and −1.48 percentage points, and evaluate the KDE at x = −2.50 percentage points with bandwidth h = 0.50 percentage points. The Gaussian estimate is f(x) = (1/n)Σ[exp(−(x−xᵢ)²/(2h²))/(h√(2π))], so its units are density per percentage point. Here n = 6 and the six component contributions are approximately 0.1111, 0.1323, 0.1111, 0.0726, 0.0394, and 0.0166 per percentage point; adding them gives f(−2.50) ≈ 0.4831 per percentage point. This is a height, not a 48.31% probability: an interval probability still requires integrating the curve over a range. As a bandwidth diagnostic, keeping these six synthetic observations fixed but changing h to 0.70 pp lowers the calculated height at −2.50 pp to about 0.4217 per pp, illustrating smoothing rather than a change in the observations. The result describes this selected sample only; it is not a forecast or causal estimate, and the truncated displayed range can omit tail area.
lessons.takeaway: Use area for interval probability, and remember that smoothing can leak across real data boundaries.

practice.question: A density curve is tallest near a 0% return. Does the curve's height give the probability of an exact 0% return?
practice.hint: A single point has zero area on a continuous scale.
practice.solution: No. The height is density per unit, not point probability. The probability of a range around zero is the area over that range.

lessons.title: Joint and conditional densities add a second variable
lessons.body:
For paired observations (xᵢ, yᵢ), a bivariate KDE can place a two-dimensional kernel at each point. With separate bandwidths hₓ and hᵧ, a product-kernel form is f̂(x,y) = (1/(n hₓ hᵧ)) Σᵢ Kₓ((x−xᵢ)/hₓ)Kᵧ((y−yᵢ)/hᵧ). The resulting surface describes joint concentration. Integrating over one variable gives a marginal density; dividing the joint density by the relevant marginal gives a conditional density. A density surface can show a relationship that a single correlation number misses, but estimates become data-hungry as dimensions increase—the curse of dimensionality.

A joint density keeps both variables paired, while a conditional density focuses on one variable at a specified level of the other. Using synthetic observations of training hours per month and hourly earnings in currency units—(2, 15), (4, 16), (4, 20), and (8, 25)—the subset at exactly 4 training hours has earnings 16 and 20, whose simple average is (16+20)/2=18 currency units per hour. A conditional KDE would smooth around 4 hours rather than automatically treating these two points as the whole population. The marginal earnings density would ignore training hours entirely. This comparison assumes the measurements are on compatible scales and enough nearby pairs exist; it does not prove that extra training causes higher earnings. For density-estimation guidance, see “Scikit-learn User Guide — Density Estimation” in the linked sources.

Consider this explicitly synthetic illustration of a conditional KDE for hourly earnings y (currency units per hour) near x = 5 monthly training hours. Suppose the paired observations are (3,18), (4,20), and (6,24), and use a Gaussian x-bandwidth hₓ = 1 hour. Their unnormalized proximity weights are exp(−2) = 0.1353, exp(−0.5) = 0.6065, and 0.6065, so the normalized weights are approximately 0.100, 0.450, and 0.450. A local conditional mean is therefore (0.100×18 + 0.450×20 + 0.450×24) currency units per hour = 21.60 currency units per hour; it is a weighted summary, not a causal return to training. If hᵧ = 2 currency units per hour and we ask for density at y = 22, the Gaussian kernel values are about 0.0270, 0.1210, and 0.1210 per currency unit, producing f̂(22|5) ≈ 0.112 per currency unit after weighting. That height is not a probability; an interval probability requires integrating over an earnings range. Results depend on both bandwidths, the local data supply, and the assumption that nearby x-values provide relevant comparisons. The three points are illustrative, not observed earnings, and this paired extension is not the lab’s one-variable return chart.
lessons.formula: f̂(x,y) = (1 / (n hₓ hᵧ)) Σᵢ Kₓ((x−xᵢ)/hₓ) Kᵧ((y−yᵢ)/hᵧ)
lessons.takeaway: A second variable changes a curve into a surface; more dimensions require much more data.

practice.question: You want to see how the distribution of fund returns changes with market returns. Which object is more relevant: the marginal density of fund returns alone or a conditional density given market returns?
practice.hint: The question asks about fund returns at different levels of another variable.
practice.solution: A conditional density of fund returns given market returns directly answers the question. A joint density can also display both variables together; a marginal density alone omits their pairing.

lessons.title: Kernel regression estimates a local conditional mean
lessons.body:
The lecture connects density estimation to the Nadaraya–Watson estimator. At a chosen x, it computes a weighted average of nearby outcomes: m̂(x) = Σᵢ wᵢ(x)yᵢ, where wᵢ(x) = K((x−xᵢ)/h) / Σⱼ K((x−xⱼ)/h). The weights add to one, so this is a local mean rather than a density. Small bandwidths focus tightly on neighbors; large ones average broadly. This nonparametric curve can describe a nonlinear conditional mean without choosing one global straight line, but it is an association estimate, not a causal effect.

The Nadaraya–Watson calculation is transparent when kernel weights are supplied. Suppose three synthetic firms have advertising spending of 1, 2, and 5 thousand currency units and sales growth of 4%, 6%, and 10%, respectively. At x=2 thousand currency units, use illustrative kernel weights 0.25, 1, and 0.05. Their total is 1.30, so normalized weights are 0.25/1.30, 1/1.30, and 0.05/1.30. The estimate is (0.25×4%+1×6%+0.05×10%)/1.30=5.77% approximately. The output remains in percent because it is a weighted average of percentage outcomes. It describes a local conditional mean, not the effect of increasing advertising by one thousand currency units; confounding and extrapolation remain concerns. For implementation details on kernel regression, see “statsmodels — KernelReg” in the linked sources.

Consider a synthetic retail example in which x is a store’s discount, measured in percentage points, and y is weekly sales measured in thousand currency units. To estimate mean sales at a 10-point discount, suppose three illustrative observations are (8, 120), (10, 150), and (13, 240), with supplied kernel weights 0.25, 1.00, and 0.10. First add the weights: 0.25 + 1.00 + 0.10 = 1.35. Normalize them to 0.1852, 0.7407, and 0.0741 (approximately), then compute the local mean: (0.25×120 + 1.00×150 + 0.10×240) / 1.35 = 204/1.35 ≈ 151.11 thousand currency units per week. The estimate is therefore a conditional mean in y-units, not a slope or a forecast for one store. A useful diagnostic is to repeat the calculation with a wider bandwidth: more distant stores receive material weight, so the estimate may move toward a broader market average. Near the edge of the observed discount range, weights are inherently one-sided, making boundary bias plausible; avoid treating the curve as reliable extrapolation beyond the available x values.
lessons.formula: m̂(x) = Σᵢ wᵢ(x)yᵢ  ·  wᵢ(x) = K((x−xᵢ)/h) / Σⱼ K((x−xⱼ)/h)
lessons.takeaway: KDE estimates where data concentrate; Nadaraya–Watson estimates a locally weighted average outcome.

practice.question: Why do the Nadaraya–Watson weights include a denominator that sums all kernel weights?
practice.hint: Compare the weights with shares that should add to one.
practice.solution: The denominator normalizes the local weights to sum to one, making the estimate a weighted mean of nearby y values.

lessons.title: Local polynomials and a careful workflow
lessons.body:
Local polynomial smoothing fits a small polynomial near each target x, weighting observations by distance. Degree zero is the local-constant Nadaraya–Watson idea; higher degrees can adapt to local slopes and often reduce boundary bias. The supplied lecture also sketches semiparametric regression, which combines a structured linear component with a smooth component for other covariates. These tools add flexibility, not automatic truth: results depend on bandwidth, sample size, covariate scaling, edge behavior, and model design. In practice, plot the raw points, label units, compare bandwidths, check boundary behavior, and keep descriptive association separate from prediction and causal claims.

A local polynomial can correct a straight-line fit’s edge behavior, but the data near the edge still matter. Imagine synthetic weekly delivery times of 2, 3, 4, and 5 days with satisfaction scores of 80%, 78%, 75%, and 70%. At x=2 days, a local constant fit may average nearby scores and flatten the endpoint. A local linear fit instead estimates a local slope: using the first two points, the change is (78−80)/(3−2)=−2 percentage points per day, so one illustrative one-day extrapolation predicts 82% at x=1 day. That prediction is outside the observed range and should not be treated as evidence. Local polynomial degree, bandwidth, and edge support must be reported; the curve is associational and does not prove faster delivery causes satisfaction. For kernel-regression implementation details, see “statsmodels — KernelReg” in the linked sources.

Consider an illustrative, synthetic wage-growth diagnostic rather than observed data. To estimate monthly wage growth at an unemployment rate of x₀ = 6 percentage points, suppose four nearby observations are (x, y) = (4, 2.4%), (5, 1.8%), (7, 1.0%), and (9, 0.2%), where y is percent per month. With a Gaussian bandwidth h = 2 percentage points, use weights wᵢ = exp[−(xᵢ−6)²/(2h²)]: approximately 0.607, 0.882, 0.882, and 0.325. Fit yᵢ = a + b(xᵢ−6) by weighted least squares. The weighted sums give Σw = 2.696, Σw(x−6) = −0.239, and the fitted coefficients are a ≈ 1.442% per month and b ≈ −0.433 percentage points of wage growth per one percentage-point increase in unemployment. Thus the local estimate at 6% is 1.44%, while the local-constant (Nadaraya–Watson) weighted mean would be 3.992/2.696 ≈ 1.480%. The small difference reflects slope adjustment, not causality. Recheck sensitivity to h and sparse support; this is interpolation near 6%, not a license to extrapolate beyond the observed range.
lessons.takeaway: Flexible smoothing is useful when the shape is unknown, but each added degree of freedom needs data and diagnostics.

practice.question: A local-polynomial curve bends around the observations. Does that establish that changing x would cause y to change along that curve?
practice.hint: Separate the shape of an observational fit from the design that supports intervention claims.
practice.solution: No. It estimates a conditional relationship. Causal interpretation still needs a credible experimental or observational identification design and its assumptions.

caseStudy: A risk analyst compares simulated daily returns for two hypothetical funds: one may contain a single broad cluster, while the other may have a quiet center and a separate shock-prone group. The analyst overlays a histogram and KDE, labels returns in percent, and compares a narrow, medium, and wide bandwidth before describing any peaks. The curve is a smoothed description of the selected sample—not a forecast, a guaranteed tail bound, or evidence that one fund caused another outcome. For an interval such as returns below −2%, the relevant probability-like summary is area over that range under the estimated density, conditional on the data and smoothing choice. All figures are educational and do not represent a recommendation.
misconceptions: A density height is not the probability of one exact continuous observation.
A KDE's peaks are not guaranteed population subgroups; bandwidth can create or hide them.
The kernel shape is not the only choice—bandwidth often changes the estimate more.
A smooth conditional curve does not prove a causal relationship or forecast the next return.
Higher-order or multivariate smoothing is not automatically more accurate, especially with small samples.

quiz.question: Which change most directly makes a Gaussian KDE smoother while leaving the observations and kernel shape fixed?
quiz.explanation: A larger bandwidth spreads each kernel across a wider neighborhood, generally smoothing local variation. It can also oversmooth real structure, so compare plausible values.
